opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest thing that gets overlooked is the question of what a world model is actually *for*. A lot of the current conversation treats world models as essentially very good next-frame predictors. You train a big generative model on video, it learns to produce plausible continuations, and the assumption is that somewhere inside it there must be a model of the world. Plausible pixels are not the same thing as understanding, though.

When I think about what makes human world models powerful, it's not that we can render the future in high fidelity. Most of us can't. It's that our models are structured in a way that supports a huge range of queries. I can ask "what would happen if I pushed this?", or "why did that fall over?", or "what would have happened if I hadn't been there?" Those are interventional and counterfactual questions. They need a model that represents causal structure: objects, agents, forces, intentions. A model that has only learned the statistical texture of observations can't answer them.

So I think the discourse conflates two things. One is predictive accuracy on some distribution of observations. The other is having a model you can reason with: one you can condition, intervene on, and invert to explain what you're seeing. Video generation benchmarks mostly measure the first. Science, planning, and real generalization need the second.

The other thing that gets overlooked is that world models aren't fixed. Humans build them on the fly. You walk into a new situation, a new game, a new lab, and within minutes you've constructed a working model of how things operate there, tested it with a few experiments, and revised it. That active, hypothesis-driven process of model *construction* is, to me, the core of intelligence. The question isn't just "do you have a world model?" It's "can you build the right model for this situation, quickly, from little data, and know when it's wrong?"

That's where I think probabilistic programming and causal reasoning still have a lot to offer. I don't mean them as a replacement for deep learning. I mean them as a way to think about what structure we want these systems to have. Scale has given us remarkable perceptual and generative capabilities. Whether scale alone gives us models we can genuinely reason with, especially out of distribution, is still very much an open question, and I'd like to see the field take it more seriously than it does now.

r001.rationale: The response discusses causal structure and building models for new situations, but does not state that the same system can be understood through world models at different levels of abstraction.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes models suited to prediction from models suited to reasoning, and connects those differences to tasks such as video benchmarks, science, and planning.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the thing that gets overlooked is that "world model" has quietly become two different concepts wearing the same name, and people argue past each other because of it.

One version is the deep learning version: a world model is whatever latent state a network builds up that lets it predict the next frame, the next token, the next observation. And by that definition, sure, large models have world models. They have to, to predict as well as they do. But that's a very thin notion. It's really just saying "compression that generalizes," and I don't think it captures what people actually care about when they use the phrase.

The other version, which I'd say is closer to the original meaning, is that a world model is something you can reason over. It's not just a predictor. It's a model you can intervene on, ask counterfactuals of, hold fixed in one place while you vary something else. The question isn't "can it predict what happens next," it's "does it have an object that represents the world such that you can do things with that object other than roll it forward." Simulation, inference, planning, explanation, all of those are operations on the model, and they're different operations. A pure next-step predictor collapses them all into one.

So the thing the discourse misses is that representation and inference have been conflated. People talk about whether a model "has" a world model, as if that's a binary property of the weights. But the interesting question is what inferences you can run against it. Can you condition on something you didn't train on? Can you ask what would have happened under a different intervention? Can you express uncertainty over the structure itself, not just over outcomes? Those are questions about the interface, about what the model affords, not about whether some representation is hiding in there somewhere.

And the second thing I'd say, which follows from that, is that there's an assumption that world models should be learned end to end, from pixels or tokens up. I'm skeptical of that as the whole story. Humans don't learn physics from scratch every time they walk into a new room. We have abstractions, objects, causes, agents, that are nearly universal, and we compose them. The hard problem isn't learning the model, it's learning the right language to write models in, so that when you encounter something new, you can construct a model of it quickly, with very little data, and the model is something you can actually inspect and reason about. That program synthesis flavored view of world modelling, where the model is a program and learning is partly search over programs, is almost absent from the mainstream conversation right now, and I think it's where a lot of the real difficulty lives.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes two meanings of “world model,” but does not clearly state that the same system can be understood through world models at different levels of abstraction.

r002.rationale: It lists different operations and questions one might apply to a model, but does not state that which world model is useful depends on the task.

astra-6.text:
I think one thing it overlooks is what we actually want a world model to do. Predicting what happens next is one thing. Being able to ask, “What would happen if I intervened?” or “Why did this happen rather than something else?” is another. A system can be very good at prediction without having the causal structure you need to answer those questions reliably.

And then there’s the question of whose model, and for what purpose. We often talk about a world model as though there’s one complete representation of reality that we’re trying to recover. But useful models are selective. They leave things out. The right abstraction for controlling a robot might be very different from the right abstraction for helping someone understand a scientific result.

So I’d like to see more attention paid to how we specify those abstractions, how we test them, and how people can inspect and revise them. What matters isn’t just whether a model produces something plausible, but whether we can use it to reason about a particular question—and recognize when it doesn’t know enough to answer.

r001.rationale: The response describes different abstractions for different purposes, but does not clearly state that the same system can be understood through world models at different abstraction levels.

r002.rationale: It says the useful abstraction depends on the purpose, contrasting robot control with helping someone understand a scientific result.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we often talk about a world model as though it were simply a system that predicts what happens next. But prediction leaves open a lot of questions. What are the objects in the model? What counts as an intervention? Can you ask what would have happened if you’d acted differently, and get an answer for the right reasons?

You can be very good at predicting observations without having the causal structure you need to make decisions. If I watch someone else interact with a system, that doesn’t necessarily tell me what will happen when I intervene myself.

So I’d like the discussion to be more explicit about what we want these models to support. Predicting video, explaining an event, planning an action, and reasoning about a counterfactual are related capabilities, but they impose different requirements. Calling all of them “world modelling” can obscure the interesting questions about how they fit together.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes several capabilities and their requirements, but does not say that one system can be modeled at different levels of abstraction.

r002.rationale: It says models should be evaluated by what they need to support and that prediction, explanation, planning, and counterfactual reasoning impose different requirements.
